Topic: KV cache eviction policy sensitivity to prompt structure variability in long-context inference serving

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-922)
response:
The central question is: given a fixed KV cache budget, how does the distribution of prompt structures arriving at an inference server — not just their lengths — determine whether eviction policies like LRU, LFU, or sliding-window actually preserve the tokens that matter for generation quality? A KV cache stores the key-value attention tensors computed for prior tokens so they don't need recomputation; when the cache fills, some entries must be evicted, and the choice of which entries to drop is the policy. The beginner thinks about this as a memory management problem — analogous to CPU cache replacement — but the expert knows that attention weight distributions are highly non-uniform and prompt-structure-dependent: a retrieval-augmented prompt front-loads critical context that a sliding window will happily evict, while a few-shot prompt has token importance concentrated in specific example boundaries that neither LRU nor LFU can detect without attention score instrumentation. The deeper worry is cross-request interference in a shared cache: when prompts are structurally heterogeneous (some are long system prompts, some are chat histories, some are document-stuffed RAG queries), the eviction policy optimized for one structure class systematically degrades another, and this interaction is invisible in per-request benchmarks but surfaces as tail latency and quality degradation in production distributions. Experts also worry about the feedback loop: eviction decisions made at serving time affect which tokens get recomputed, which changes GPU utilization, which changes batching decisions — so a locally reasonable policy can produce globally unstable throughput under load.

In a concrete RAG prompt — say, a 16K-token context with a 512-token system prompt, 8 retrieved passages of ~900 tokens each, and a 200-token query — an oracle policy would unconditionally protect the system prompt tokens and the query tokens, then selectively protect the 2-3 passage spans whose content words have high lexical overlap with the query, because those are the spans the decoder will actually attend to during generation. LRU fails here for a structural reason: the system prompt and retrieved passages were written to cache early in the request, making them the oldest entries — precisely the ones LRU evicts first under pressure, even though they are the most reuse-critical. Attention-score-based policies (as explored in systems like ScissorHands, 2023, and SnapKV, 2024) fail for a subtler reason: they sample attention weights from prefill passes on earlier layers or earlier requests to predict what future decode steps will attend to, but RAG prompts exhibit cross-passage attention suppression — the model attends broadly during prefill to locate relevant spans, then narrows sharply during decode, and the prefill signal is a poor proxy for decode-time importance. SnapKV specifically reports that naively using prefill attention to select KV entries to keep causes accuracy degradation on multi-hop reasoning tasks because intermediate "bridge" tokens — conjunctions, coreference anchors, and passage boundary markers — receive low prefill attention scores yet are load-bearing for coherent generation. The numbers matter: H2O (Heavy Hitter Oracle, Zhang et al. 2023) showed that even retaining the top 20% of tokens by cumulative attention score still drops 5-8% on downstream QA metrics for retrieval-heavy prompts, because the heavy-hitter heuristic conflates attended-to tokens with necessary tokens. The oracle's advantage is that it has access to the full generation trajectory and can identify the minimal sufficient set of KV entries retrospectively — a signal that no online policy can compute without speculative or deferred execution.

Reuse distance — the number of distinct cache entries accessed between two accesses to the same entry — is the canonical theoretical lens here: Mattson et al.'s stack distance formalism (1970, still the foundation) proves that LRU is optimal if and only if the reuse distance distribution is well-approximated by a stack distribution, meaning future accesses are drawn from a stable, time-invariant popularity ranking. In a heterogeneous LLM serving stream, you would almost certainly observe a heavy-tailed mixture distribution — a combination of a near-zero spike (system prompts and shared prefixes reused across hundreds of requests), a middle mass (session-scoped chat histories reused a handful of times), and a long flat tail (one-shot RAG contexts never reused at all) — and this shape is the fingerprint of non-stationarity, meaning the popularity ranking shifts depending on which request class is arriving. The critical implication is that any static policy is theoretically suboptimal for a mixture distribution: LRU is near-optimal for the middle mass but catastrophically wrong for the spike (it evicts the most-reused system prompt because it appears old) and wastes budget on the tail (it retains RAG tokens that will never be accessed again). Systems like RadixAttention in SGLang (Zheng et al. 2024) implicitly acknowledge this by using prefix-tree matching to give near-infinite effective reuse distance to shared prefixes — essentially hand-coding oracle behavior for the spike component — but they leave the tail and middle mass to LRU, accepting suboptimality there. Empirically, vLLM's PagedAttention traces (Kwon et al. 2023) show that in production ShareGPT workloads, the top 5% of unique prefixes account for over 60% of cache hits, which is a power-law concentration consistent with the spike-plus-tail shape and confirms that a policy blind to prefix identity will waste most of its budget. The shape therefore delivers a precise verdict: no static policy can be optimal across all three components simultaneously, and the theoretical minimum requires either workload classification at admission time or an adaptive policy that detects distribution shift online — the gap between what SGLang achieves on the spike and what remains unaddressed on the tail is a direct measure of how much performance is left on the table.

The concrete mechanism is attention sink plus local window collapse: during prefill of a RAG context, attention mass distributes across three structurally distinct zones — the initial sink tokens (positions 0-3, which capture disproportionate softmax mass as shown in StreamingLLM, Xiao et al. 2023), the query-proximal tokens (the final ~200 tokens before generation), and a sparse set of semantically relevant passage spans in the middle — but current eviction policies see only a flat sequence of KV pages and have no representation of this three-zone structure, so under memory pressure they evict middle-passage pages uniformly, which destroys the sparse relevant spans alongside the genuinely ignorable ones. The defeating mechanism is specifically the variance in importance across the middle zone: in an 8-passage RAG context, 6 passages may contribute near-zero attention during decode while 2 contribute over 70% of cross-attention mass, but this 6:2 ratio is not knowable from token position, recency, or prefill attention alone because which passages are relevant depends on the query, and the query's interaction with passages only becomes legible at the final layers of the prefill pass — after the KV tensors for those passages have already been committed to cache. SnapKV (Li et al. 2024) operationalizes a partial fix by pooling attention scores from the last 16 query tokens across prefill layers to vote on which KV positions to retain, achieving roughly 1.2× memory reduction with under 1% accuracy drop on single-hop QA — but their own ablations show the method degrades on multi-hop tasks because the voting signal is corrupted by attention diffusion across bridge tokens. The instrumentation you would need to reliably detect intra-request importance before generation is: (1) a lightweight router that classifies incoming prompt structure (RAG vs. chat vs. code) to set policy parameters, (2) per-layer attention entropy measurement during prefill to identify which layers show the sharpest query-passage alignment signal (typically layers 16-24 in a 32-layer model), and (3) a query-passage similarity prescore — either BM25 or a small embedding model — computed at admission time to pre-rank passages before prefill even runs, so the cache manager has a prior on which page slots are eviction candidates. The fundamental instrumentation gap is that all current systems commit KV pages to cache during prefill, before the final-layer attention signal is available, meaning any policy that wants to use that signal must either buffer and retroactively evict (adding latency) or speculate using earlier-layer proxies (adding error) — and no production system has yet closed this loop with acceptable overhead.

The failure mode has a name in the retrieval literature — the "lexical chasm" — and it is most acute for inferential bridges: passages that do not share vocabulary with the query but provide a definitional, causal, or analogical link that the model needs to chain reasoning steps. The practical handle on this is to treat the prescore not as a hard ranker but as a prior that gets updated by a cheap proxy inference signal: specifically, you can run a single forward pass through only the first 8 layers of the model (which costs roughly 25% of full prefill compute for a 32-layer model) and read out the cross-attention entropy at layer 6-8, which is cheap enough to do before committing KV pages and informative enough to catch inferential bridges that surface early in the attention stack — this is the intuition behind the "early exit" probing literature (Schuster et al. 2022 on confident adaptive transformers, though not applied to KV caching directly). A second handle is diversified eviction budgeting: rather than evicting the bottom-ranked passages entirely, you retain a compressed KV representation of every passage — dropping, say, 75% of each low-scored passage's tokens rather than 100% — which preserves the bridge structure at lower resolution and gives the decoder something to attend to if the prescore was wrong; this is architecturally similar to what PyramidKV (Cai et al. 2024) does by allocating fewer KV slots to lower layers where attention is diffuse, repurposed here across passages rather than layers. The numbers on how often this matters are sobering: on MuSiQue (a multi-hop QA benchmark), Trivedi et al. 2022 showed that roughly 30% of correct answers require a bridge passage that shares zero unigrams with the question, meaning a lexical prescore would rank it last in nearly a third of hard cases. The deeper systems insight is that this is fundamentally a risk management problem under uncertainty: you have a budget, a prior (prescore), a likelihood update (cheap partial forward pass), and an asymmetric loss function (evicting an inferential bridge is catastrophically worse than retaining a useless passage), so the optimal policy is a Bayesian budget allocation that never zeros out any passage but concentrates eviction on high-confidence irrelevant spans — and the practical implementation is a two-threshold system where passages above score τ₁ get full retention, passages below τ₂ get maximum compression, and the middle band gets partial compression with a retroactive eviction hook if decode-time attention confirms irrelevance.

In vLLM's PagedAttention, KV cache is allocated in fixed 16-token blocks managed by a CPU-side block table, and mid-generation eviction requires: (1) a CPU-GPU synchronization point to update the block table, (2) a scatter-gather reindex of the attention kernel's block pointers for the affected sequence, and (3) if the system is running continuous batching, a potential stall on the batch scheduler because block table mutations are not atomic with respect to the prefill/decode iteration boundary — empirically this synchronization overhead runs 50-200 microseconds per eviction event on an A100, which is 5-15% of a single decode step latency for a 7B model at batch size 1, and compounds badly at batch size 32+ where the scheduler must reconcile block table state across all concurrent sequences. Fragmentation is the subtler cost: PagedAttention was specifically designed to eliminate external fragmentation by using fixed-size blocks, but retroactive mid-generation eviction reintroduces internal fragmentation because you evict whole 16-token blocks even when only 4-6 tokens within the block are the actual targets — meaning your effective eviction granularity is coarser than your importance estimation granularity, and you discard useful tokens alongside useless ones at a ratio that depends on block size versus passage boundary alignment. The break-even calculation changes substantially once you account for these costs: if speculative pre-eviction at admission time carries a 2% accuracy risk on inferential bridge cases (roughly the MuSiQue failure rate for aggressive lexical prescoring), and retroactive eviction costs 10% decode latency overhead plus fragmentation waste of ~30% of the intended memory savings, then pre-eviction is worth the accuracy risk for any workload where the bridge-failure rate is below ~2% and latency SLOs are tight — but inverts for multi-hop-heavy workloads where bridge failures occur in 25-30% of requests, making the accuracy cost dominate. Attacc (Wang et al. 2024) and InfiniGen (Kim et al. 2024) both attempt to amortize this by prefetching partial KV blocks from CPU to GPU speculatively during decode, which reframes the problem from eviction-and-recompute to offload-and-fetch — but their reported fetch latency of 1-3ms per block on NVLink systems still exceeds the retroactive eviction synchronization cost, meaning offloading only wins when the evicted blocks are large and the generation is long enough to amortize the fetch. The practical upshot is that block size is a hidden policy parameter: vLLM's default 16-token block size was chosen to minimize paging overhead for normal operation, but it is the wrong granularity for importance-based mid-generation eviction, and a system that wanted to make retroactive eviction cheap would need sub-block addressing — which reintroduces the external fragmentation PagedAttention was designed to eliminate, creating a genuine architectural tension with no free solution.

A ground-up design would abandon fixed-size blocks in favor of a two-level addressing scheme: a coarse allocation tier using 64-128 token "segments" aligned to natural prompt structure boundaries (system prompt, each retrieved passage, query), and a fine eviction tier using 4-token "atoms" within segments that can be individually tombstoned without freeing the segment's virtual address range — this is structurally similar to how jemalloc handles size-class segregation, and it would let importance-based eviction operate at atom granularity while the allocator manages fragmentation at segment granularity, eliminating the mismatch that makes PagedAttention's 16-token blocks too coarse for token-level importance signals. The attention kernel would need to be rewritten to handle sparse segment maps — essentially a compressed sparse row (CSR) format for the block pointer table — which FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al. 2024) partially enables through its support for variable-length sequences and custom masking, but production CSR attention kernels currently run 15-30% slower than dense block attention on H100s due to irregular memory access patterns that defeat the tensor core's assumption of aligned 16×16 tile operands. To resolve the fragmentation tradeoff, the system would use a slab-style reclamation policy: when atom-level evictions within a segment exceed a threshold (say, 60% of atoms tombstoned), the segment is compacted — surviving atoms copied to a fresh segment, old segment freed — amortizing compaction cost across many decode steps rather than paying it per-eviction, analogous to log-structured storage compaction in RocksDB. The new failure modes introduced are qualitatively different from PagedAttention's: first, compaction creates latency spikes during generation when a heavily-evicted segment triggers a copy operation mid-decode, potentially adding 500μs-2ms jitter that is invisible in throughput benchmarks but violates p99 latency SLOs; second, the structure-aligned segment boundaries require a prompt parser at admission time, and parser errors (misidentified passage boundaries, malformed prompts) produce catastrophically wrong segment maps that cause the importance estimator to operate on the wrong granularity — a silent correctness failure with no exception to catch. Third, and most insidiously, the two-level scheme's correctness depends on segment boundaries being stable across the request lifetime, but techniques like speculative decoding and prompt compression (LLMLingua, Jiang et al. 2023) mutate the effective token sequence mid-request, invalidating the segment map and requiring either a full remap (expensive) or stale boundary metadata (incorrect eviction decisions). The design is strictly more powerful than PagedAttention for importance-aware workloads but introduces operational complexity — parser maintenance, compaction tuning, boundary stability guarantees — that PagedAttention entirely avoids by treating all tokens as structurally identical, which is precisely why no production system has shipped it despite the theoretical advantages being clear since at least the H2O paper in 2023.

The cleanest metadata-free design is a learned eviction policy that operates directly on KV tensor statistics — specifically, the L2 norm and mean absolute value of each token's key vector — without any structural labels, because key vector magnitude has been empirically shown to correlate with attention sink behavior and query relevance (Ge et al. 2023, FASTGEN) and is computable atomically per-token without cross-token structural context. This approach is essentially what ScissorHands (Liu et al. 2023) approximates: it observes that tokens with persistently high attention scores across early decode steps tend to maintain that property, so it uses a small fixed-size "observation window" of decode steps to build a per-token importance score from raw attention weights alone, with no prompt structure assumptions — the policy degrades gracefully when structure is absent or corrupted because it never assumed structure to begin with. The sacrifice is precise and quantifiable: without structural metadata, the policy cannot distinguish between a high-norm token that is important because it is a query anchor versus one that is important because it is an attention sink at position 0-3 — both look identical to a magnitude-based eviction rule, so the system over-retains sink tokens and under-retains semantically critical middle-context tokens, which FASTGEN reports as a 3-5% accuracy gap on long-context retrieval tasks compared to structure-aware methods. A second sacrifice is eviction timing: structure-aware systems can make eviction decisions at admission time using segment boundaries as natural decision points, but a metadata-free system must wait for decode-step attention signals to accumulate before it has reliable importance estimates, meaning it cannot free memory until 10-20 decode steps have elapsed — during which it may have already exhausted cache budget and been forced to recompute or stall. The most principled metadata-free design would combine key-vector statistics with a lightweight online learning component — a per-request bandit or exponential moving average over token importance scores — that adapts to the actual attention distribution as generation proceeds without ever needing to know why that distribution has the shape it does; Luo et al.'s work on dynamic sparse attention (2024) moves in this direction but has not been applied to eviction policy specifically. The fundamental sacrifice of all metadata-free approaches is the same: they trade predictive eviction (act before memory pressure using structural knowledge) for reactive eviction (act after observing attention patterns under memory pressure), and in a tight-budget serving system that difference in timing is the difference between graceful degradation and forced recomputation.
